q: Matter is composed of atoms which are very small in size.
e: All matter is fundamentally composed of extremely small particles called atoms.

q: An atom consists of a core called the nucleus around which the particles called protons are moving in orbits.
e: An atom consists of a nucleus around which the particles called electrons are moving in orbits.

q: An electron is a negatively charged particle having a charge of $-1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.
e: The electron carries a negative charge with a magnitude of $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.

q: The nucleus consists of two kinds of particles called proton and neutron.
e: The atomic nucleus is composed of positively charged protons and uncharged neutrons.

q: A proton is a positively charged particle and a neutron is an uncharged particle.
e: Protons carry a positive charge, while neutrons have no electric charge.

q: An electron and a proton have the same magnitude of electric charge.
e: Although their signs are opposite, the magnitude of the charge of an electron and a proton is identical.

q: The nucleus has net negative charge.
e: The nucleus has a net positive charge due to the presence of protons.

q: The magnitude of positive charge of the nucleus is equal to the sum of the positive charges of all the protons present in the nucleus.
e: The total positive charge of the nucleus is the sum of the charges of all its constituent protons.

q: In a normal atom the number of orbiting electrons is always equal to the number of protons.
e: A normal, uncharged atom maintains an equal number of protons and electrons.

q: Since the magnitude of positive charge of the nucleus is equal to that of the total negative charge of electrons, a normal atom has no net charge.
e: The equal and opposite charges of protons and electrons cancel each other out, resulting in no net charge.

q: A normal atom is said to be electrically neutral.
e: Because it has no net electric charge, a normal atom is electrically neutral.

q: If an atom gains one or more electrons, it carries a positive charge.
e: If an atom gains one or more electrons, it carries a negative charge due to the excess of negative particles.

q: If an atom loses one or more electrons, it becomes positively charged.
e: Losing electrons leaves the atom with more protons than electrons, resulting in a net positive charge.

q: When an atom becomes a charged atom, it is called an ion.
e: A charged atom, whether positive or negative, is referred to as an ion.
